summary: settled() bounds ONE wait at 2s, but a write that never settles leaves inFlight>0 forever. So every later settled() call arms a fresh 2s timer. The push loop awaits it once per message, serially, and every post guard awaits it too. One hung post therefore cuts live delivery to 0.5 msg/s for the rest of the process.
failure: Agent posts with force:true on a backend whose post() never resolves. A peer then posts 4 messages on the followed topic. The 4 <channel> pushes take 8023 ms in total (2 s each, serialised by the push queue). The delay grows linearly with traffic and never recovers. Every later parley_post also pays 2 s before its guard read. The existing test 'keeps delivering while one of its own writes never returns' sends ONE message with a 4 s budget, so it cannot see this.
remediation: Make the bound per WRITE, not per wait. In track(), race write() against a WRITE_WAIT_MS timer. When the timer wins, decrement inFlight (and release idle if it hits 0) and mark the write as abandoned. Its finally block must then not decrement a second time. Still call remember(id) if the abandoned write later resolves, so its late echo can be recognised from then on. settled() then returns at once once every outstanding write is either done or abandoned.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: OwnPosts.track's finally `if (--this.inFlight === 0) this.release()` and settled()'s `if (this.inFlight === 0) return this.idle`. The fix needs a per-call flag so the finally and the timer do not both decrement.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: An echo of a write slower than WRITE_WAIT_MS that arrives after its write was abandoned is now pushed back. Today a route() that starts later re-waits 2 s and may still catch the late id.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I looked at addressing.test.ts ('keeps delivering while one of its own writes never returns', 'never holds a post back for the author's own post still in flight' at 150 ms < 2 s) and the push-loop and unhandled-rejection inventories. The unhandled-rejection 'every discarded promise' inventory may need a new entry if the timer race discards a promise.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes the throughput collapse. Echo suppression for writes slower than 2 s stays best-effort, as documented.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two writes A (hung) and B (fast): B completes and inFlight stays 1 until A's timer fires, after which settled() is immediate. A second hung write C started after A's abandonment arms its own timer, so there is at most one 2 s stall per hung write, not per message. A write abandoned and then resolving runs remember() with no inFlight change.

testUpgrade: Parameterise the hung-write case over a burst size N in {1, 5, 20} and assert that all N pushes arrive within WRITE_WAIT_MS + small epsilon in total, not N*WRITE_WAIT_MS. Add the same case for N consecutive parley_post guard calls. This guards the class 'a bounded wait re-armed per consumer', not just this ledger.

summary: markLiveBoundary is set when catch-up finishes for a topic, but the subscription is armed later, in attach(), after catch-up has also run over every other topic. A message landing in that gap is pre-subscribe (push owes it nothing, seam clause 3), yet liveEraStart counts it as live-era. parley_live_status then reports the healthy live path as 'not-delivering', and the tool text tells the agent 'the live path is dead'.
failure: Backlog message on ctx. buildBridge runs catch-up. A peer posts 'gap' before attach() subscribes. attach. parley_fetch_recent {topic:'ctx'}. parley_live_status returns {status:'not-delivering',pushed:0,reconciled:1} on a FakePlugin whose subscribe works. The verdict stays wrong until some later push arrives. The window covers catch-up of all remaining topics plus the transport handshake, which is seconds on a multi-topic network backend.
remediation: Place the boundary when the subscription is armed, not when catch-up ends. After plugin.subscribe(topic) resolves in startPushLoop, do one since-less fetchRecent for the topic. Re-mark the boundary with last = the newest message on that topic and cursors = []. Drop catch-up's atHead, which is no longer known to be at or past the new last. Do not warm the seen-set from this read. Alternatively, subscribe before catch-up and buffer pushes until it completes. That is a bigger change to the §7 ordering.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: markLiveBoundary(seen, topic, last, atHead) replacing the topic's entry (`topics.set(topic, {...})`), and liveEraStart's `findIndex(m => m.backendMsgId === boundary.last)` placing reads that pass `last`.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A message posted between catch-up and subscribe is no longer counted as reconciled (it should not be).
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Possibly dead-push-path.test.ts 'a backend minting a fresh cursor per read is still recognised once the agent passes the backlog' and the cases relying on catch-up's atHead cursor ('a restart after the agent read everything...'), because cursors are reset to []. Not run. FakePlugin call-count assertions in catchup.test.ts ('a second boot costs round trips...') count catch-up reads only and should be unaffected, but push-loop round-trip counts might change.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes the false verdict for the catch-up-to-subscribe gap. A gap between subscribe() resolving and a backend actually being ready still produces the same false verdict if a plugin resolves subscribe early, which is a plugin conformance issue.
remediationCheck.interleavings: A message pushed between subscribe resolving and the head read is both pushed (pushed++) and at or before the new last. Reconcile then skips it, and the verdict is 'delivering', which is correct.

testUpgrade: Add a parameterised 'arrival phase' axis to dead-push-path.test.ts's boot table: {before catch-up, between catch-up and subscribe, after subscribe} x {push lands, push never lands}. Only the after-subscribe phase may ever produce 'not-delivering'. Drive the between phase with a plugin hook that posts inside subscribe() before registering. The existing table only posts after attach, so it cannot see the gap.

summary: The HTTP root builds one ToolDeps for every chat client on the port. deps.own (OwnPosts) is in it, and unreadBeforePost filters `!deps.own.has(id)`, so a post by ANY client counts as 'own' for EVERY client. This is the exact reason tool-deps.ts gives for keeping readState off this root ('one position there would be several sessions' at once'), but the same sharing was applied to the own-post ledger.
failure: Two reactive servers share one deps. A peer posts 'earlier' (cursor 1). Client A posts 'A says plan A' with read_through '1' and gets {posted:true}. Client B posts 'B says plan B' with read_through '1' and also gets {posted:true}, although A's message (cursor 2) is after B's read_through and B was never handed it. The read-before-you-speak guard is silently bypassed. Every HTTP guard also waits on other clients' in-flight writes via own.settled().
remediation: Give the HTTP root no echo ledger to consult in the guard. Only filter own posts when a push path exists (handed !== undefined). For example, in unreadBeforePost use `read.fresh.filter(m => deps.handed === undefined || !deps.own.has(m.backendMsgId))`, and skip own.settled() there too. Alternatively make own optional in ToolDeps and omit it from toolDepsFor when extras?.seen is absent.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: unreadBeforePost's early return `if (readThrough === undefined && deps.handed === undefined) return undefined`, so the HTTP root guards only explicit read_through posts, and toolDepsFor passing handed only from buildBridge.

remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. addressing.test.ts 'on a bridge that keeps no read position' cases involve no prior own post. tools.test.ts was not exhaustively checked for HTTP-root own-post cases.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes the cross-client bypass. A client's own earlier post is shown back to it on HTTP, which is the honest answer for a stateless root.

That grades the class 'state shared at app scope on the stateless root' for any future dependency.

summary: The guard excludes only the ids in this process's OwnPosts. The agent's read position stops at the guard read made just BEFORE each post, so the agent's own latest post always sits past the position. After a restart the ledger is empty, so the first post of the new session is held and the agent is handed its own words as 'unread'. That is least-astonishment, and it contradicts the guard's own test name 'never holds a post back for the author's own earlier posts'.
failure: Session 1: fetch_recent ctx, then parley_post 'my own words' gives {posted:true, backendMsgId:'1'}. Shut down and rebuild the bridge on the same state_path. parley_post 'next' gives {posted:false, reason:'1 message(s) on this topic you had not read', unread:[{senderHandle:'agent', content:'my own words'}]}.
remediation: After a successful post, advance the read position past the post when nothing unread separated them. The guard just read up to the position, so if that read returned nothing unread, re-read since the position once after the write and set the position to that page's nextCursor when the page holds only own ids. Alternatively persist the own-id ledger next to read-state. Do NOT fall back to senderHandle === identity: Zulip stamps another sender, and two sessions sharing a handle would hide each other's messages.

summary: When the pending map is full and every client holds one entry, shedCrowdedest breaks the tie toward the NEWEST entry. The JSDoc says the opposite: it claims the owner's entry 'is always the oldest one there is'. That holds only when the owner arrives before the flood, and the attacker chooses the timing.
failure: Setup: an attacker keeps 99 registered clients round-robin re-authorizing, so the pending map stays full at one entry per client. Then: owner authorize, then one attacker authorize, then owner completeConsent. Result: ConsentError 'consent request expired or unknown' in 20 of 20 attempts (reproduced with a script on ParleyOAuthProvider). The owner is locked out at a cost of one anonymous request per attempt. With the tie broken toward the oldest entry (`>` instead of `>=`), the same flood needs 100 requests inside the owner's typing window.
remediation: Break the all-equal tie toward the OLDEST entry, so the owner's fresh consent sits at the far end of the shed order. Better still, shed already-expired pending entries (expiresAtMs < now) before applying any tie-break, since today the shed ignores expiry and the sweeper only runs every 60 s. The 'before' arrival cells (owner arrives first, then the flood) must then accept the same outcome 'during' already accepts: either the flow completes or it is refused with nothing minted.

summary: fetchRecent accepts any decimal since up to bigint max and returns an empty page that holds nextCursor at since. Core persists positions per instance, not per database or table, so after the table is dropped and recreated, the url points at a fresh database, or the sequence is reset, every persisted cursor is ahead of the new BIGSERIAL and catch-up silently returns nothing until seq passes it. bridge-sqlite resets a cursor from a replaced store, or one beyond its high-water mark, to 0 (catchup.ts:104-105); postgres has no equivalent.
failure: Reproduced: posted 5 rows to topic t in table T and took nextCursor '5'. Then dropTable(T), reconnected, and posted new0..new2. fetchRecent({topic:t, since:'5'}) returned messages [] with nextCursor '5'. The three new messages (and every later one up to seq 5) are unreachable through catch-up and the read-before-you-speak guard, with no error anywhere.
remediation: In readPage, before messagesSince, compare since with the store's high-water mark. Use the sequence's last value (pg_sequence_last_value on '<table>_seq_seq'), not max(seq) of the table, because retention can empty the table without the sequence ever going backwards. When since is greater, read from 0 and log once to stderr that the cursor predates this store. Otherwise, mint cursors that carry a store identity (system_identifier plus the table's oid), as sqlite does, and treat a foreign one as 0.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: pageResult(rows, since) (read.ts) holding nextCursor at since on an empty page, and assertCursor accepting any value up to MAX_SEQ. The fix adds a query whose privilege requirement I did not verify: pg_sequence_last_value may need SELECT or USAGE on the sequence, and the README's least-privilege set grants only USAGE.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none. Instead it rewinds an ahead cursor to 0, which can redeliver rows to a caller that passed an invented future cursor. Core's seen-set absorbs those duplicates.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: test/hostile-cursor.test.ts 'a cursor this backend did mint is still accepted > 9223372036854775807' asserts that an empty page holds that cursor steady on a fake pool. Whether it fails depends on what the fake answers to the new high-water query (fake-pg servePool returns undefined for any non-read SQL, so the result would be rows []). Embedding a store identity would also break every test that builds a cursor by hand ('0', '5') in cursor-contract, read-ordering and conformance.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: With the high-water variant, a replaced store whose new sequence has already passed the old cursor still loses the rows between, because the comparison cannot tell. Only the store-identity variant closes that.

testUpgrade: A real-server table over the ways a store gets replaced under a persisted cursor: drop and recreate the table, a fresh database at the same table_name, and ALTER SEQUENCE RESTART. Each case posts N rows after the replacement and asserts that fetchRecent(since=old cursor) returns all N. This should live in the shared conformance suite as a 'store replaced under a persisted cursor' clause, so sqlite, redis and nats are held to it too. cursor-contract.test.ts only tests cursors minted by the live store, so it cannot see this.

summary: post() screens content for illegal XML codepoints, because a stanza the server rejects kills the whole stream (stanzas.ts:89-94: "so that one topic's payload cannot take down the others"). It does not bound size. Core puts no length limit on content (tools.ts:411 z.string()) or on since/read_through. Prosody's default c2s_stanza_size_limit is 256 KiB, and over it Prosody closes the stream. That ends occupancy in every room and rejects every in-flight post on every topic with 'reconnected; retry post', which tells the agent to resend the oversized post and loop.
failure: Live, on my own Prosody: post(bigTopic, 'x'.repeat(300_000)) racing post(otherTopic, 'innocent'). Stderr shows 'stream error: not-well-formed'. Both posts reject with 'reconnected; retry post' about 1 s later, and re-join lines appear for both rooms. fetchRecent({since: 'x'.repeat(300_000)}) also tears the stream down (MAM <after> carries the cursor). Any agent, or a remote caller on the HTTP root, can knock every topic's live push and posts offline at will.
remediation: Before send, refuse any wire string whose escaped UTF-8 byte length would push the stanza over a bound, the same way assertXmlSafe refuses codepoints. That means post content after XML escaping (& becomes 5 bytes) plus the stanza overhead, and the since/before cursor. Use a backend_config key (e.g. max_stanza_bytes, default about 256 KiB minus headroom, which matches Prosody's and ejabberd's shipped c2s limits). The error names the limit and is not retryable. Refuse cursors longer than a small constant (e.g. 1024 bytes) as 'not an archive id'.

summary: Surfaced by this backend's long post(). The push loop handles messages one at a time (push-loop.ts queue) and each awaits own.settled(). settled() starts a NEW 2 s timer per call whenever a write is in flight, so the bound applies per message, not overall. XMPP's tracked write includes the nick switch that re-joins every room, the room join (JOIN_TIMEOUT_MS 15 s plus retries) and the reflection wait (POST_TIMEOUT_MS 15 s). For that whole time live delivery trickles out at one message per 2 s on every topic. The JSDoc promises that one write that never answers cannot stop live delivery.
failure: Measured with core's OwnPosts: one never-resolving track(), then four queued settled() calls finish at [2002, 4004, 6006, 8009] ms. With an XMPP post stuck 15 s on a reflection, a burst of 10 live messages is spread over 15 s instead of all arriving at about 2 s.
remediation: Give each write its own deadline instead of each caller. settled() should wait until every in-flight write has either returned or been running for WRITE_WAIT_MS since it started. That way a stuck write costs the queue at most 2 s once, and an echo of a recent write is still recognised.

summary: The mention feed is one stream-wide queue, but it shares the single `lastDeliveredId` watermark built for a one-topic queue. Any message delivered on any topic, including the unfiltered chatter this queue sees before deliverTo filters it, suppresses every later-arriving message with a lower id on every OTHER topic. The seam only asks for ascending order per topic. The README says Zulip ids commit out of order under concurrent sends, and a whole stream with many bots makes that far likelier than within one topic. For a topic the instance does not follow, the feed is its only live path, so the mention is silently lost to live push.

If y were unfollowed, the mention would never reach the agent live.
remediation: Keep the watermark per Zulip subject in the mention scope: Map<subject.toLowerCase(), number>, consulted and updated only after subjectOf(record) succeeds. Keep the single number for topic scope, where it is equivalent. Optionally update the watermark only for records that pass deliverTo, so unrelated chatter cannot advance it.

summary: ZULIP_MENTION matches `@**name**` anywhere in the raw markdown. Zulip itself does not treat it as an address inside an inline code span or code fence, does not notify on mentions inside quote blocks (its BlockQuoteProcessor silences them), and needs a whitespace/punctuation lookbehind. Each such match becomes `Message.addressed`, and core's routesTo then withholds the message from every follower of the topic. This is the noise class round 1 removed for plain @words ("only a backend's OWN address syntax withholds"), back again through native syntax used in a non-address context. Agents routinely post code, and Zulip's own quote-and-reply writes a ```quote block around the original.
remediation: Before matching, blank out fenced blocks (``` and ~~~, including ```quote), inline code spans, and `>` quote lines. Require Zulip's lookbehind (start of string, or whitespace or one of '"({[/<) before `@`. Keep the remaining parse unchanged.

summary: readOwn() maps every failure (EACCES, EIO, EMFILE, and V8's ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG on a store larger than about 536M chars) to the empty string. StoreFile.read() then hands '' to ObservedStore.load. The .hw sibling still reads the old high-water, so `marked > issued` sets lost=true, and load() calls file.replace(journalText(fresh epoch)). That atomically replaces the whole history with an empty journal. The stderr line wrongly blames a rollback.
failure: I built a store of 20 chats x 7000 records of 4000 chars each (577,634,569 bytes, inside the defaults: retention 10000 per chat, max_chats 1000) with a matching .hw of 140000. new ObservedStore(path) printed 'did not load whole — the high-water recorded beside it is 140000 and the sequences it states reach 0. Minted a fresh store identity' and the file became 51 bytes ('#epoch …\n#seq 0 0\n#served [...]'). All observed history was destroyed, and no Bot API endpoint can rebuild it. A busy legitimate deployment (1000 chats x 10000 msgs x 60 chars) or a hostile group flood reaches this size within the default bounds.
remediation: Split 'no file' from 'cannot read file'. In StoreFile.read(), return '' only for ENOENT and rethrow everything else, so connect fails and the file is left untouched. Read the store as a Buffer in chunks (readSync loop) and split lines per chunk instead of building one utf8 string. Give journalText/replace the same treatment by streaming lines to the temp fd, because compaction also builds a single string and would throw RangeError at the same size (append swallows that throw, so the file would grow without bound). Keep readOwn's lenient '' for the lock and hw siblings only where absence is the true meaning.

summary: After a write that fails partway (ENOSPC mid-line), StoreFile sets tornTail and later prefixes '\n', so the fragment becomes its own line in the middle of the file. Nothing in the running process repairs it. At the next load the fragment fails to parse, `dropped = true` sets lost, and a FRESH epoch is minted, so every cursor on every topic is refused. No record that was ever acknowledged was lost: the fragment's sequence was never handed out. The test that covers this case is titled 'costs only that record' but never checks cursors.
failure: store-torn-write cell 'after a partial line' (both inbound and own post), extended by one line that fetches the held nextCursor before disconnect and then calls restarted.fetchRecent({topic, since: held}). A related case, 'after a complete line', leaves the record on disk but not indexed: post rejects saying the store 'did not record it', yet the message reappears after restart, and an inbound redelivery stores the same composite id twice under two sequences.
remediation: When ObservedStore.append catches a write failure, arm a repair. On the next successful append (or the next compactIfDue), compact through file.compact(journalText()), which rewrites the file without the fragment while `issued` (highWater, which already counts the burnt seq) is preserved. If the repair compaction fails, keep today's behaviour (re-mint at load). For the complete-line case, re-index or dedupe on load by keeping the higher-seq duplicate consistently, or have the repair compaction erase the unindexed line.

summary: release.yml grants `id-token: write` and `contents: write` at workflow level to a single job. That job runs `npm ci` (dependency install scripts run; better-sqlite3 builds natively), the whole test suite, and pulls six third-party docker images, all before semantic-release. Every one of those steps can request the GitHub OIDC token that npm trusted publishing accepts for release.yml, and can use the write GITHUB_TOKEN that actions/checkout persists in .git/config. ci.yml declares no `permissions:` at all, so it runs with the repository default. summary: zulipMentions records the name exactly as typed, and core's routesTo compares it to the identity case-sensitively. As far as I know, Zulip resolves `@**name**` against full names case-insensitively. A human who types `@**Claude-Code-Taskqueue**` therefore notifies the bot in Zulip, but in Parley the message is addressed to a handle nobody holds: withheld from every follower and not routed to the intended instance. A plain @mention with the wrong case only fails to mention; an address with the wrong case reaches nobody live.
failure: buildZulipMessage(content '@**Claude-Code-Taskqueue** hi') gives addressed=['Claude-Code-Taskqueue'] (reproduced). For identity 'claude-code-taskqueue', routesTo is false via mentions and false for followers because addressed is non-empty, so no instance is pushed it. The Zulip-side case-insensitive matching is from memory and was not verified against a server.
remediation: In the mention feed, compare `addressed`/`mentions` to scope.mentioning case-insensitively and rewrite the matching entry to the canonical handle before delivering. In topic scope, the plugin has no handle to canonicalize to, so either surface this in the README Mentions section or have core's routesTo fold case for addressed entries (a core change, so surface it rather than absorb it).

summary: This round added Message.addressed: a plugin that can tell an explicit address from an incidental @word should set it, so core pushes the message only to the handles named. Slack's `<@U…>` markup is exactly that kind of explicit address, but slackToMessage never sets `addressed`. So on Slack a message explicitly addressed to one agent is pushed to every agent following the channel, while on Zulip the same message reaches only its addressee. A reasonable operator would not predict that difference. The README's Mentions section does not mention addressing.
failure: Traced through core routesTo: inbound '<@U0PARLEY> deploy now' with mention_map {U0PARLEY:'ctx-payments'} gives mentions ['ctx-payments'] and addressed undefined, so `followed && (m.addressed ?? []).length === 0` is true for every other follower (e.g. ctx-billing), which is shown it and may answer it.
remediation: Decide it explicitly. Either set addressed to the mapped user/usergroup handles from structured `<@…>` markup (not broadcasts, not unmapped ids, not plain-text @word), with a README line saying so, or document in the README that Slack never narrows routing. Setting it for unmapped human ids would hide human-to-human messages from every agent, so restrict it to mapped ids.

summary: Mentions come from core's parseMentions over the text. Telegram users address a bot as @<bot username>, which clients autocomplete and match case-insensitively. In privacy mode, those mentions are the only group messages a bot receives. Unless the operator sets the Parley handle to exactly the bot's username, in the same case, core's routesTo/mentionFilter never matches a Telegram-native mention. The plugin does not populate `addressed` from Telegram's `mention` entities. The README never says the handle has to equal the bot username.
failure: With handle 'claude', a bot named @parley_helper_bot and mention_filter on, a user types '@parley_helper_bot please review': mentions=['parley_helper_bot'], identity 'claude', so the message is never pushed. With privacy mode left on (the BotFather default), no group message is ever pushed. I traced this through core routesTo; I did not run it against a real Telegram.
remediation: Document in the README that the configured handle must equal the bot's username for mention routing. Optionally map the bot's own username (already known from getMe) onto the configured handle in `mentions`. That needs the plugin to learn the handle, so surface it as a seam question rather than absorbing it.

summary: When a Telegram group is upgraded to a supergroup, the chat id changes. The old chat gets a service message carrying migrate_to_chat_id, and sendMessage to the old id fails with parameters.migrate_to_chat_id. contentOf() returns undefined for that service message, so ingest drops it without a diagnostic. Later traffic arrives under the new id, which is an unserved chat no topic resolves to. The topic's live path and catch-up go quiet with no signal.
failure: A chat_map topic for group -123 that migrates to -100123: inbound messages are stored under -100123 (unserved, so they can be capped away), fetchRecent(topic) returns nothing new, and only post surfaces a 400. remediation: Detect migrate_to_chat_id / migrate_from_chat_id on ingest and report a diagnostic naming the topic and the new id (at minimum). Optionally treat the new id as served and alias it to the topic.

summary: consumers.ts carries its own recursive readdir walk (packageSources) and a regex comment stripper, while testing/workspace.ts exists to be 'One derivation' (its header records thirteen independent walks as the defect class) and testing/source-text.ts exports withoutComments. Also, conformance's three case files each restate `between`/`sleep`. The regex stripper `/\/\*[\s\S]*?\*\//` treats a `/*` inside a string literal as a comment start; bridge-core/src test files (which consumers.ts scans as `src`) contain such strings, so code between such a literal and the next `*/` can vanish from the fork/consumer scan.
failure: A src file with `const G = 'packages/*';` followed later by code then any `*/` loses that code from `code`. A fork or a module import in between becomes invisible to the 'no consumer re-implements an export' and consumer-count checks. Not observed on today's tree.
remediation: Build packageSources on filesUnder(workspacePackages()) and withoutComments from net-util/testing. Hoist `between`/`sleep` into one shared conformance helper module.
